questions.question: Ravi draws a rectangle that is 3 cm tall and 152 cm wide. He cuts it into three smaller rectangles that are all 3 cm tall, with widths of 100 cm, 50 cm and 2 cm. What is the total area of the whole rectangle?
questions.explain: Multiply each part by 3 and add all three partial products: 100 × 3 = 300, 50 × 3 = 150, 2 × 3 = 6, so 300 + 150 + 6 = 456 square cm. The most common trap is leaving out the middle part and only adding 300 + 6.

questions.question: Maya makes an area model for 213 × 4. She draws a rectangle 4 cm tall and 213 cm wide, then splits the width into 200 cm, 10 cm and 3 cm. What is the area of the whole rectangle?
questions.explain: Each strip is 4 tall, so the partial products are 200 × 4 = 800, 10 × 4 = 40 and 3 × 4 = 12; adding all three gives 852. If you get 842, you wrote the 2 from 12 but forgot to regroup the extra ten.

questions.question: A paper strip for a classroom border is 6 cm wide and 143 cm long. Noah splits the length into 100 cm, 40 cm and 3 cm so he can use an area model. Which expression shows the areas of his three parts added together?
questions.explain: The distributive principle says every part of the length must be multiplied by the width, so you need 6 × 100, 6 × 40 and 6 × 3 all added. Two traps: dropping one of the three partial products, and using the bare digits 1, 4 and 3 instead of their real values 100, 40 and 3.

questions.question: Priya builds an area model for 316 × 3. She draws three parts that are all 3 cm tall, with widths 300 cm, 10 cm and 6 cm. Then she writes 900 + 18 = 918 square cm. What went wrong?
options: Nothing went wrong; 900 + 18 = 918 square cm is right
She left out 1 × 3 = 3, so the area is 921 square cm
She left out 10 × 3 = 30, so the area is 938 square cm
She left out 10 × 3 = 30, so the area is 948 square cm
questions.explain: An area model for a 3-digit number always has three partial products: 300 × 3 = 900, 10 × 3 = 30 and 6 × 3 = 18, giving 900 + 30 + 18 = 948. The tens part is the one children skip most often, and it is worth 30, not 3.

questions.question: Use partial products to find 407 × 6.
questions.explain: Break 407 into 400 + 0 + 7: 400 × 6 = 2400, 0 × 6 = 0 and 7 × 6 = 42, so the product is 2442. Watch two traps here — zero times 6 is 0 (not 6), and the 4 tens from 42 must be regrouped, not dropped.

questions.question: Each of the 3 Grade 5 classes at a Burnaby school collected 268 cans for a food drive. How many cans did they collect altogether?
questions.explain: Split 268 into 200 + 60 + 8: 200 × 3 = 600, 60 × 3 = 180 and 8 × 3 = 24, so 600 + 180 + 24 = 804. The trap is losing the tens: forgetting the regrouped ten from 24 or skipping the 180 both make the answer too small.

questions.question: A hockey stick costs $128 at a Richmond sports store. Ravi's team buys 5 of them. What is the total cost?
questions.explain: Use partial products on 128 × 5: 100 × 5 = 500, 20 × 5 = 100 and 8 × 5 = 40, so the total is 500 + 100 + 40 = $640. If your answer is smaller than $640, check that you added all three partial products and carried the tens from 8 × 5 = 40.

questions.question: Three water tanks at a Kelowna campground each hold 342 litres when full. All three are full, and campers use 26 litres in the morning. How many litres of water are left?
questions.explain: First multiply: 300 × 3 = 900, 40 × 3 = 120, 2 × 3 = 6, so 342 × 3 = 1026 litres; then subtract, 1026 − 26 = 1000 litres. The trap is doing the subtraction on a total that is missing the 120 from the tens part.

questions.question: Jayden works out 254 × 3 with partial products. He writes 600 + 12 = 612. What is his mistake and what is the correct product?
options: He left out 50 × 3 = 150, so the product is 762
He left out 50 × 3 = 150, so the product is 750
He forgot to regroup, so the product is 652
questions.explain: A 3-digit number has three parts, so 254 × 3 needs 200 × 3 = 600, 50 × 3 = 150 and 4 × 3 = 12, giving 762. Jayden jumped from the hundreds straight to the ones — always check that you have one partial product for every digit.

questions.question: A tree-planting crew near Prince George plants 175 seedlings each day for 4 days. Their goal for the week is 800 seedlings. How many more seedlings do they still need to plant to reach the goal?
questions.explain: Step 1: 100 × 4 = 400, 70 × 4 = 280, 5 × 4 = 20, so 175 × 4 = 700 seedlings. Step 2: 800 − 700 = 100 more. The big trap is regrouping — 5 × 4 = 20 and 7 × 4 = 28 both carry, and losing either carry makes the total far too small.

questions.question: A strip of lawn beside a school field is 8 m wide and 124 m long. A gravel path already covers 200 square metres of that strip. How many square metres of lawn are left?
questions.explain: Find the area first with partial products: 100 × 8 = 800, 20 × 8 = 160, 4 × 8 = 32, so the strip is 992 square metres; then 992 − 200 = 792 square metres of lawn. Skipping the 160 or dropping a regrouped ten makes the area too small before you even subtract.

questions.question: Aanya says, “To find 236 × 5, I can do (200 × 5) + (36 × 5).” Ben says, “You have to do (200 × 5) + (30 × 5) + (6 × 5).” Who is right, and what is 236 × 5?
options: Only Aanya is right, because Ben splits 236 into too many parts
Both are right, but the total is 1050
Both are wrong; the correct way is (200 × 5) + (6 × 5) = 1030
Both are right — each split adds back to 236, and both give 1180
questions.explain: The distributive principle works for any split whose parts add back to the whole number, so 200 + 36 and 200 + 30 + 6 both give 1000 + 180 = 1180. The real error to avoid is a split that loses a part, like leaving the 30 out and getting 1030.
